A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SAFE-NET research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies can be identified and do not constitute missing material.

before.justification: v1 reports original PDE benchmark errors, training curves, runtime comparisons, optimizer and feature-count studies, and Hessian spectral analyses.

after.justification: v2 reports original PDE experiments, revised benchmark comparisons, additional component ablations, optimizer studies, and quantitative Hessian analyses.

M1.justification: The adaptive Fourier features, domain features, centered normalization, and single hidden layer remain. However, the reported loss changes from the unweighted residual, boundary, and initial-condition terms in v1 Appendix A.1 to explicit weights of 1, 100, and 100 in v2 Appendix A. Expanded feature-extraction and forward-pass descriptions otherwise clarify the existing method.

E1.justification: v2 adds a separate forced diffusion task, replaces the 1D heat problem with 2D anisotropic heat, and replaces steady 2D Allen–Cahn with time-dependent 1D Allen–Cahn. Wave frequency, convection velocity, and Navier–Stokes Reynolds number also change. v1's 'Diffusion' case matches v2's 'Reaction' by initial condition and stated logistic solution, despite an inconsistent equation in v2; that renaming alone is not new coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparisons replace adaptive-activation A-PINN with first-layer-sine FLS-PINN and add RBA-PINN with Fourier embeddings. v2 separately evaluates RBF and RBF-P. Since v1's RBF-PINN implementation already included ten polynomial terms, the polynomial variant has a predecessor; the additional pure-RBF comparison expands membership. RFF-PINN becoming RFF is only a renaming.

E3.justification: The primary comparison changes from 150,000 Adam epochs to 40,000 iterations comprising 30,000 Adam and 10,000 L-BFGS iterations. Restart schedules gain learning-rate tuning and revised second-phase rates. Spectral analysis changes from 40,000 hybrid-optimizer iterations to 100,000 Adam-only iterations to address optimizer confounding. RBF bandwidth changes from problem-specific tuning to a reported fixed value of 1.0.

E4.justification: v1 mainly studies feature count, optimizer switching, and spectra. v2 adds activation, frequency-initialization, coefficient-initialization, network-depth, and normalization ablations in Appendix C.1. Appendix A.3 substantially expands optimizer-schedule comparisons across methods and PDEs, while Appendix C.3 adds quantitative spectral comparisons. These test previously unexamined design and stability questions.

E5.justification: v2 newly reports five random initializations or seeds per experiment and explicitly states averaging for initialization ablations. v1 supplies no corresponding run counts. This establishes additional replication reporting, not an increase from a known earlier count. The numerical tables still lack accompanying standard deviations or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Benchmark scores are extensively replaced and new optimizer, ablation, and spectral results are added. v1 Table 3 places SAFE-NET first or second on every task; v2 Table 3 places it third on Allen–Cahn and Burgers and fourth on Navier–Stokes. These comparisons use revised tasks, settings, and baselines, so they do not establish same-setting regression. Table 1 also changes SAFE-NET's reported parameter count from 5.8k to 6.8k.

T1.justification: The central Fourier and NTK eigenvalue derivations in Sections 3.1 and 6 are retained. Local mathematical changes include removing v1's RBF composed-kernel Taylor derivation and adding RBA multiplier bounds in v2's baseline appendix. v2 also drops the factor u from the retained reaction equation while preserving its logistic solution, introducing a mathematical inconsistency.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows 'orders-of-magnitude lower errors' to general error improvement, and the contribution list removes the claim of theoretical demonstration of preconditioning. Benchmark superiority is qualified as holding 'on average.' v2 also adds parameter-efficiency claims relative to large architectures and revises the claimed average parameter saving against feature-engineering baselines from 65% to 53%.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive explanations connecting L-BFGS failures to random-frequency mismatch and adaptive NTK weighting, and explains Allen–Cahn's sharp interfaces as a difficulty for Fourier features. New ablation interpretations distinguish normalization's role in optimization stability from the smaller benefits of additional depth. The existing high-dimensional scalability limitation and broad discontinuity caveats remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds PyTorch and GPU specifications, collocation and boundary sample counts, sampling instructions, dataset provenance, explicit feature-selection rules, and a complete forward-pass description. It expands baseline implementation and tuning details and specifies PyHessian-based spectral estimation with 100 stochastic samples and 200 Lanczos iterations. Many of these are newly disclosed details rather than established changes in execution.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around compact feature-engineered models versus large PINNsFormer, PirateNets, and operator-learning architectures. It adds substantive discussion of RBA's Fourier component, SIREN-inspired activations, and polynomial-enhanced RBFs. New references also document PDEBench, PINNacle, initialization methods, and spectral-computation tools.

P1.justification: The introduction and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten, and experiments are organized around explicitly numbered optimization schedules. The general PDE formulation moves from the appendix into the introduction. Existing setup material is reorganized into common settings, systematic feature-extraction rules, a forward-pass specification, and expanded method-specific subsections.

P2.justification: v2 replaces the introductory heat plot with a wave plot, redesigns the performance summary into best- and median-competitor comparisons, expands baseline table columns, and adds blue highlighting for near-best results. Numerous optimizer and component-ablation displays and quantitative spectral tables are added. Existing material is also relocated or redisplayed, including the retained architecture diagram and duplicated main benchmark results in the appendix.

improvement.justification: Expanded baselines, component ablations, reproducibility details, and Adam-only spectral controls address weaknesses in v1. However, v2 introduces material inconsistencies: Schedule (1) Allen–Cahn error is 1.97e-3 in Tables 3 and 5 but 9.97e-4 in Table 4; Tables 5–6 show RBF-P improving on every task despite the claim that only SAFE-NET does so. Appendix B also contains inconsistent reaction and diffusion equation–solution pairs. These gains and reporting problems prevent a confident judgment of net overall improvement.
